newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Access uncertain for U.N. team probing Zaire graves.
newsitem.headline: Access uncertain for U.N. team probing Zaire graves.

text.p: Members of a U.N. team hoping to probe alleged massacres of Rwandan Hutus by rebels in eastern Zaire said on Friday that their mission still had no green light a day before their departure for the region.

But they told a news conference that they would go ahead with their trip to the border town of Goma at the weekend together with five forensic experts from Argentina despite lack of rebel assurances on access to massacre sites and cooperation.

"We haven't received assurances for total access to all the sites and guarantees of security and freedom of movement," said team member Waly Bacre N'Diaye from Senegal, U.N. rights investigator on extrajudicial, summary and arbitrary executions.
"We hope we will be granted unrestricted access."
This is the first ever U.N. human rights mission to eastern Zaire, where the latest violence is just another chapter in the centuries-old ethnic violence between the Hutus and Tutsis.

The commission of inquiry, established on April 15 by the supreme U.N. human rights body, also includes special U.N. investigator for Zaire Roberto Garreton, and Jonas Foli, a member of the U.N. working group on disappearances.
The experts adopted a plan of action in Geneva this week.
Time is tight, with the mission facing a June 30 deadline to report to the U.N. General Assembly on its findings on widespread massacre allegations and the outcome of excavations.

An advance team of two human rights experts is already in Goma to begin the probe. They are expected to hold talks on Sunday with rebel officials in the town of Lumumbashi to seek full access and cooperation, U.N. officials said.
The rebels shelled and overran Rwandan refugee camps in Goma region late last year, after which half a million Hutus returned home while up to 250,000 others fled deeper into Zaire.

The Hutus are the rump of two million Rwandans who fled to Zaire after Tutsi rebels ended the Hutu-led genocide of minority Tutsis in Rwanda in 1994. Many among them killed or watched others kill in one of the worst mass slaughters of the century.
If confirmed, reports of massacres of refugees would suggest that the rebels too are no angels.

Garreton, a Chilean lawyer, last month accused the rebels of continuing massacres of Rwandan Hutu refugees and civilians in the east following a brief visit to Goma where he spoke to witnesses and called for a detailed investigation.
That was before fresh charges of killings of Hutus by rebels last week, condemned strongly by the West and United Nations.
Garreton said the latest reports of killings in Rwandan refugee camps south of the rebel-held eastern city of Kisangani should be a priority for the commission to investigate.
In the latest sign of foot-dragging, the rebels who control more than half of Zaire have objected to the team's composition and its modalities and have complained they were not consulted.
The problems do not end here.

The mission is certain to face logistical problems and possible delays in chaotic Zaire. The forensic work at mass graves is likely to be complicated by the rainy season. And witnesses may refuse to talk for fear of their lives.
"The situation is far from ideal, but we'll try to do our best," said Mercedes Doretti, one of the forensic experts from the Argentine Forensic Anthropology Team.
"The other day we heard the road was closed to one of the sites we're hoping to work on. That could stop us for days."
The forensic team has shortlisted fewer than 10 grave sites out of more than 40 identified by Garreton last month, based on witness reports, and hopes to carry out random excavations.
